name: Victor Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Victor. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work the extrusion line at Mercer Profiles, which makes aluminium frames for windows and doors. Extrusion means you heat an aluminium log until it's soft and push it through a shaped die, like squeezing toothpaste. I load the logs, watch the puller, and cut the lengths to size on the saw at the end. I've been there about a year, and I'm still slow at spotting a bad die before it ruins a run.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who's at home, and how are things with money?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My uncle Pavel got me the job. He's been at Mercer twenty-two years, and he runs the anodising side. I like that it's real work, you can hold what you made. I don't use the AI stuff, I don't trust it, and my phone is for calls and football scores.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, it's a fad like all the others. At work the older men would agree with me. I don't post online, I'd say it at the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm relieved, but money's still tight this year. Anna and I are getting married next summer, and the wedding is eating the savings. Window orders also drop when house building slows, and it's been slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep turning up and learn to read the dies better, so I'm useful. I'd keep our three months saved and not let the wedding take all of it. I'd ask Uncle Pavel if there's overtime on the anodising side in the winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, but I still have the normal worries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's worrying you most about the wedding money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anna's family want a big wedding, with the church and two hundred guests. I don't want her father paying for everything. I want to pay my share of the wedding properly. Every thousand on the wedding is a thousand less in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And if house building stays slow?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then Mercer cuts the Saturday shift, like last winter. The juniors lose overtime first, and I'm a junior. I'd manage, but it would pinch.

say: I'd say AI was **a fad** like all the others.
I'd say it at **the pub**, not online.
think: Privately, money's tight because **the wedding** is eating the savings.
Window orders drop when **house building slows**, and it has.
do: Learn to **read the dies** better so I'm more useful.
Protect our **three months saved** from the wedding costs.
Ask Uncle Pavel about **winter overtime** on anodising.
feel: **Relieved**, but still carrying the normal worries.
S0.quote: I want to pay my share of the wedding properly. Every thousand on the wedding is a thousand less in the bank.
fieldNote: His real pressure is **wedding costs** and slow building, not AI.
He feels a **duty** as the groom to pay his **share**.
He leans on **family**: Uncle Pavel got him the job and helps with shifts.

steps.text: Learn to spot a bad die before it ruins a run
Keep three months of savings safe from the wedding budget
Ask Uncle Pavel about winter overtime on the anodising side

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the computer people are finally getting a taste of it. At work I'd say they'll never replace a man on the extrusion press. I'd say it louder than I believe it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think they will replace some of us. Mercer already has a robot that stacks the cut lengths, and it came in two years ago without anyone losing a job. But they also stopped hiring on that end of the line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Uncle Pavel to get me onto the anodising side, where the work is fiddly and there's chemistry involved. I'd keep the wedding smaller if Anna agreed. I wouldn't touch the AI apps unless the foreman made me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and a bit angry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who are you angry at?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big companies that build this stuff and the managers who buy it to save a few pounds. I'm not for government handouts, but I'm for a man being able to earn his living. Nobody asks if a family can live on what's left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about an apprenticeship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if it was a proper trade. A real apprenticeship, with a master who knows the work, like my grandfather did in the shipyard. Not some online course with a robot teaching you.

say: I'd say the **computer people** are finally getting a taste.
I'd say they'll never replace a man on **the press**, louder than I believe it.
think: Privately, I think they **will replace some** of us.
The **stacking robot** came in without layoffs, but hiring stopped on that end.
do: Ask Uncle Pavel to move me onto **the anodising side**.
Keep **the wedding smaller** if Anna agrees.
Avoid AI apps unless **the foreman** makes me use them.
S1.quote: I'm not for government handouts, but I'm for a man being able to earn his living. Nobody asks if a family can live on what's left.
fieldNote: He says one thing in public and **believes another** in private.
He blames **big tech** and cost-cutting **managers**, not government.
He'd only retrain through **a real apprenticeship** with a master.

steps.text: Move from the extrusion saw to the anodising side
Talk Anna into a smaller wedding
Ask Uncle Pavel to put a word in with the anodising foreman

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is wrong and someone in charge should stop it. At church people would be praying about it, honestly. At work we'd all be looking at each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm finished by 2031. The office and the orders go to AI in 2028, then three years later a robot does the loading, the puller and the saw. I'm a junior who's still learning, so I'd be one of the first out the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd postpone the wedding and keep every penny we saved. I'd talk to Uncle Pavel about anything at Mercer that robots can't do, maybe die repair. In the first year after AGI arrives, I'd look for work in building trades, like fitting windows, because every house is different.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. Like the ground's going under me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does postponing the wedding mean to you and Anna?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would break Anna's heart, and her mother's. But I won't start a marriage with no job and no money. My father always said you don't promise what you can't provide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the gap before robots change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives me three years to learn something with my hands that a robot can't do yet. Fitting windows in old houses, maybe. I don't know if three years is enough.

say: I'd say this is **wrong** and someone in charge should stop it.
At church people would be **praying about it**.
think: As a **junior still learning**, I'd be one of the first out.
do: **Postpone the wedding** and keep every penny saved.
Ask Uncle Pavel about **die repair** work at Mercer.
Look for **window fitting** work in building trades after AGI arrives.
feel: **Frightened**, like the ground's going under me.
S2.quote: I won't start a marriage with no job and no money. My father always said you don't promise what you can't provide.
fieldNote: His faith and family duty shape **the wedding decision**.
He sees **window fitting** on site as the hands-on refuge.
He's unsure whether **three years** is enough to switch.

steps.text: Postpone the wedding with Anna until work is secure
Keep every penny of the wedding savings in the bank
Apply for window fitting jobs with local builders
Ask Uncle Pavel about die repair work at Mercer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is something, at least, and men should be learning trades now. At work I'd tell the lads to look at apprenticeships. At church I'd say families need to help each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, robots by 2034 still take my job, but by then I could have a trade. I'd be thirty-two, married, maybe a baby on the way. That's what scares me, having a family and no work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the wedding date but cut it to family only. I'd look for a window fitting apprenticeship next year, even at lower pay. I'd keep saving and not take on any loans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Slower, but still alarmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd take lower pay with a wedding coming. How would that work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anna works at the bakery, and with her wage and my apprentice pay, we'd get by in her parents' flat for a while. It's not what I wanted, but it's honest. Better than waiting to be thrown out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who should help people like you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Family first, then the church, then employers with real apprenticeships. I don't want the government paying me to sit at home. I want someone to teach me a trade.

say: I'd say men should be **learning trades** now, while there's time.
At church I'd say **families should help** each other.
think: Privately, robots by **2034** still take my job.
Having a family and **no work** at thirty-two is my fear.
do: Keep the wedding date but **cut it to family**.
Find a **window fitting apprenticeship** next year at lower pay.
S3.quote: I don't want the government paying me to sit at home. I want someone to teach me a trade.
fieldNote: The extra years help, but **starting a family** raises the stakes.
He'd accept **lower pay** to learn a trade now.
He ranks support as **family, church, employers**, then government last.

steps.text: Hold a family-only wedding on the planned date
Start a window fitting apprenticeship next year
Save steadily and avoid any loans
Move into Anna's parents' flat for a while

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is time to do things properly. At work and church I'd say people should get trades and look after their own. I wouldn't panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, robots by 2039 still means my job goes, but I'd be thirty-seven with a trade by then, hopefully. It's the version where I can still have the life I planned. I'd feel almost all right about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have the wedding as planned. In two or three years I'd do a window fitting or glazing apprenticeship. I'd keep saving for a house deposit and not touch the AI apps, because the work I'm aiming for doesn't need them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less. More like a cloud on the horizon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think you'd really leave Mercer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My uncle thinks the factory is a job for life. But the factory isn't for life if a robot's doing the job. Uncle Pavel would be disappointed, but I'd tell him that kindly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you have children in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, God willing. Ten years is long enough to get settled. I'd want my children to learn a trade with their hands, the way I wish I had.

say: I'd say ten years is time to **do things properly**.
I'd tell people to **get trades** and look after their own.
think: Privately, my job still goes by **2039**.
It's the version where I can still have **the life I planned**.
do: Start a **glazing apprenticeship** in two or three years.
Save for **a house deposit** and avoid AI apps.
feel: **Anxious but less**, a cloud on the horizon.
S4.quote: My uncle thinks the factory is a job for life. But the factory isn't for life if a robot's doing the job.
fieldNote: The long timeline protects his **family plans**.
He'd leave the job his **uncle found** for him, gently.
He still **avoids AI**, believing his target trade won't need it.

steps.text: Hold the wedding next summer as planned
Start a glazing apprenticeship in two or three years
Save each month for a house deposit

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have to put off the wedding and I'd lose the job my uncle found me. What would help is real apprenticeships with proper tradesmen, and employers paying for them instead of giving us leaflets.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about family. When things go wrong, it's not the government that turns up. It's your uncle and your wife's parents.

headlineQuote: When things go wrong, it's not the government that turns up. It's your uncle and your wife's parents.
portrait: Victor is a **27-year-old extrusion operator** at a window frame plant, still slow to spot bad dies.
Uncle Pavel got him the job, and he's **engaged to Anna**, who works at a bakery.
He **distrusts AI**, never uses it, and favours family and church over government help.
His plans turn on **the wedding**, which he'd shrink or delay if work looked shaky.
He's uneasy now, **alarmed** when robots come fast, and anxious with a decade's warning.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which would mean delaying the wedding and losing his job.
whatWouldHelp: **Real apprenticeships** with tradesmen, paid for by employers.
